title: A Stack That Tracks Its Own Minimum
statement:
Scanning the whole stack to find its minimum every time `getMin()` is
called works, but it is O(n) per call on a structure whose other
operations are all O(1). Keeping a **second** stack, storing the running
minimum alongside every push, turns `getMin()` into an O(1) lookup too --
as long as it stays exactly in step with what has actually been pushed
and popped.

## Your class

Complete `Solution`, a stack of `int`s supporting:

```
public void push(int value);
public void pop();
public int top();
public int getMin();
```

All four run in **O(1)**. `pop()`, `top()` and `getMin()` are never called
on an empty stack -- every operation sequence in a test leaves at least
one element before calling any of them.

## Watch out

- **A value that *ties* the current minimum still has to be pushed onto
  the min-tracking stack, not skipped.** The condition for pushing onto
  it is `value <= currentMin`, not `value < currentMin`. Skip the tie and
  the min-tracking stack ends up with only one entry for two equal
  minimums; pop the more recent of those two equal values back off the
  main stack, and the min-tracking stack pops its *only* record of that
  minimum away with it -- even though an equal value is still sitting
  right there on the main stack.
- **`pop()` on the main stack has to pop the min-tracking stack too, but
  only when the value being removed is the current tracked minimum.** A
  popped value that was never the minimum should leave the min-tracking
  stack untouched -- popping it unconditionally on every `pop()` call
  desynchronises the two stacks after the first element that was pushed
  without also being pushed onto the min-tracking stack.
- **Compare against the min-tracking stack's own top when deciding
  whether to push a new value onto it**, not against some other stored
  value -- `mins.peek()` is always "the minimum as of right now", which is
  exactly the number a newly pushed value needs comparing against.
